Question: An arbitrary circle can intersect the graph of \(y=\sin x\) in
Solution:
A circle centered high above the \(x\)-axis can have many positive sine peaks inside it while neighboring sine zeros lie outside. Each passage from outside to inside and back forces two intersections.

To make this precise, set
\[
L=19\pi,
\qquad R=\frac{L^2+1}{2}>0,
\]
and take the circle
\[
x^2+(y-R)^2=R^2.
\]
A point \((x,\sin x)\) lies on this circle exactly when the continuous function
\[
F(x)=x^2+\sin^2x-2R\sin x
\]
is zero. Positive values mean the point is outside the circle, and negative values mean it is inside.

For each integer \(k=1,2,\ldots,9\), one positive sine arch has zeros at
\[
a_k=2k\pi,
\qquad b_k=(2k+1)\pi,
\]
and a peak of height \(1\) at \(t_k=(2k+\tfrac12)\pi\). At the two zeros,
\[
F(a_k)=a_k^2>0,
\qquad F(b_k)=b_k^2>0.
\]
At the peak, \(0<t_k<L\), so
\[
F(t_k)=t_k^2+1-2R=t_k^2-L^2<0.
\]
By continuity, \(F\) must equal zero at least once in \((a_k,t_k)\) and at least once in \((t_k,b_k)\). These eighteen open intervals are disjoint, so they give at least \(18\) distinct intersection points.

Thus a circle can intersect the sine graph in more than \(16\) points, choice E.
